newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Hungary hospital acts to prevent infanticide.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hungary hospital acts to prevent infanticide.

text.p: Three-month old Gabor Pesti miles in his cot, unaware that he may never learn his current name and is lucky to be alive.
On March 27 Gabor was left at the entrance to a Budapest hospital in an incubator provided specifically for mothers who are too desperate to keep their children.
"We named him Gabor Pesti," said Doctor Emoke Seress. "Gabor was the nearest boys' name day on the calendar and the baby was found in the Pest side of the city."

Seress is in charge of a controversial Hungarian programme launched a year ago by the Schopf-Merei Agost hospital to tackle a rising rate of infant death from abandonment at a time of post-communist social upheaval.
The programme is creating a lot of interest in other hospitals, Seress said. Experts in Hungary and the United States and Poland have asked for information.

"We want to prevent infanticide," Seress told Reuters. "This is a programme to save children and also mothers. Pregnant women have been known to commit suicide just because they couldn't face having a baby."
PROBLEM OF ABANDONED BABIES
Seress says that some 25 infanticides a year are registered by the police in Hungary, but she believes the real figure may be 10 times higher.
Abandoned babies are generally found in dustbins, nylon bags left in deserted places or at the doors of buildings.
"The idea of our programme was that we believed the mothers may spare the babies' lives if they had the opportunity to leave them at a safe place and remain unidentified," Seress said.
"The hospital offers mothers the chance to bring babies to the hospital rather than leaving them at the local church door."

The idea originally came from Budapest deputy mayor Andrea Szolnoki. "I think the baby-saving programme has been absolutely successful," she said. "The police say that the number of children left in dustbins has dropped."
INFANTICIDE RISING IN CLIMATE OF SOCIAL DECAY

Schopf-Merei is located in Bakats square, in the very heart of Budapest on the border between the commercial centre of the prosperous fifth district and the run-down eight and ninth, where poverty and crime are at their worst.

The location is symbolic in a country which, in its headlong rush from communism to capitalism since the late 1980s, has seen living standards decline, social differences widen and crime rise at an unprecedented rate.
"Anybody can turn to us who thinks bearing a child would change her life so much she can't handle it," Seress said, adding that the hospital undertakes to keep the mother's identity secret.
The mothers who turn to the Schopf Merei are usually between 18 and 25, but some are even younger, especially girls who themselves spent ther childhood in care, she says.
But Seress stresses that the incubator is only a last resort. The programme's main priority is to help the babies begin their life in a family environment.
"In the development of personality, the creation of early devotion to someone is decisive. Without this the child starts with a disadvantage compared with others."
Since May 1996 when the programme began, more than 130 children have been born in the hospital to women who needed special care to get through pregnancy and childbirth.
MOTHERS CAN STILL CHANGE MIND AFTER GIVING UP BABY

Mothers who feel that they cannot bring up their child despite the help offered by the hospital can sign a declaration that it may be adopted and they have two months after the birth to change their mind.
Szolnoki said that almost 50 of the mothers have been convinced by the hospital that they can bring up the child and another 50 babies have quickly found adoptive parents.

The baby-saving programme simplifies an otherwise lengthy adoption process in which the baby goes first to an orphanage while government authorities go through a bureaucratic procedure to find parents.

"Only in one fifth of the cases have we not ensured a family background for the child from the beginning," Seress said. Her new job has changed her way of thinking and made her understand why a mother might abandon her own child.
"It was a shock to me that situations can occur where pregnancy is not a blessed state, a joyous moment in the life of a woman, but a real crisis which she cannot resolve," Seress said.

"It is an ambivalent feeling that I have to accept what I had regarded impossible to accept. I had to learn that." Szolnoki said the Welfare Ministry was considering extending the programme to other hospitals in Hungary.
"I feel that what we have done has been successful," she said. "Who knows where mounting tension in some of the women who turned to us could have led them?"
